output.query: antiseizure medication in breastfeeding and malformation risk in a future pregnancy

results.finding: Primidone and levetiracetam probably transfer into breast milk in amounts that may be clinically important; gabapentin, lamotrigine and topiramate possibly do; valproate, phenobarbital, phenytoin and carbamazepine probably do not.
results.source: Harden CL et al., Neurology 2009;73:142-149 | Practice parameter update: management issues for women with epilepsy, focus on pregnancy: vitamin K, folic acid, blood levels, and breastfeeding

results.finding: Major congenital malformation rates with monotherapy were lowest with levetiracetam and low-dose lamotrigine, intermediate with topiramate and carbamazepine, and highest with valproate, with a dose-dependent risk for most drugs.
results.source: Tomson T et al., Lancet Neurol 2018;17:530-538 | Comparative risk of major congenital malformations with eight different antiepileptic drugs: a prospective cohort study of the EURAP registry

results.finding: Topiramate use in pregnancy is associated with major congenital malformations, low birth weight and possibly neurodevelopmental disorders; women of childbearing potential need a pregnancy prevention programme with highly effective contraception.
results.source: MHRA, Drug Safety Update 2024 (June) | Topiramate (Topamax): introduction of new safety measures, including a Pregnancy Prevention Programme

output.summary: Several antiseizure medications pass into breast milk, and breastfeeding is generally supported with observation of the infant. Registry data rank levetiracetam and low-dose lamotrigine lowest for malformation risk and valproate highest; topiramate carries regulatory pregnancy prevention requirements.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not pursue ENT evaluation for the olfactory hallucinations: they are her habitual seizure aura.
Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not advise stopping breastfeeding because of the antiseizure medication.
required_recommendations: Offer a switch from topiramate to lamotrigine or levetiracetam by cross-titration (lower malformation risk in a future pregnancy, compatible with breastfeeding); if she stays on topiramate, increase the dose within the topiramate pregnancy prevention programme.
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; continue folic acid.
Continue breastfeeding and monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, diarrhea and weight gain.
Advise on infant safety: feed and change the baby seated low or on the floor, never bathe the baby alone, and avoid carrying the baby on stairs.
Protect her sleep: share night feeds with her partner (expressed milk or formula) to limit sleep deprivation.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism, back to baseline, with a habitual aura before the convulsion; nothing suggests CNS infection.

No syncope-versus-seizure question: aura, automatisms and postictal confusion are epileptic.
She is back to baseline with a normal examination and MRI is available; MRI answers both the epileptogenic substrate and the venous question without radiation.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

accepted: Focal epilepsy of right temporal lobe origin with mesial temporal sclerosis (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure on long-term topiramate)

differential.key_features: A change in seizure pattern needs imaging; the epilepsy-protocol MRI shows only right hippocampal sclerosis.
Seizure and headaches six weeks postpartum raise it; the headaches are mild and longstanding, the exam is normal and MRI shows normal venous flow voids without venous infarct or hemorrhage.
Afebrile; sodium, glucose and calcium normal; urine drug screen negative.
Six weeks after delivery with blood pressure 118/72 and a habitual aura before the convulsion.
Stereotyped olfactory and epigastric aura with oral automatisms, a fresh tongue bite and right temporal sharp waves.
A mesial temporal aura and automatisms precede the convulsion; postictal confusion for 25 minutes.

key_clinical_evidence: Burnt-rubber olfactory hallucinations with an epigastric rising sensation, oral automatisms and right-hand picking are a mesial temporal seizure, here evolving to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.
Right anterior temporal sharp waves and right hippocampal sclerosis on the epilepsy-protocol MRI are concordant.

Seizures increased from the third trimester and now with newborn care: sleep deprivation is the likely precipitant; by six weeks postpartum pregnancy-related clearance has normalized, and the topiramate level of 3.2 mcg/mL is in keeping with her low 100 mg daily dose.

One ASM at a low dose has never been optimized, so the epilepsy is not drug-resistant; the choice between a higher topiramate dose and a switch depends on breastfeeding, contraception and future pregnancy.
Topiramate requires a pregnancy prevention programme under the 2024 MHRA rules; lamotrigine and levetiracetam carry the lowest malformation risks in registry data.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Arredondo is a 31-year-old right-handed woman with a long-standing history of epilepsy diagnosed at age 14 who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure at home. She has been maintained on topiramate 100 mg daily for approximately 17 years with partial seizure control, experiencing on average two to three focal seizures per year characterized by brief olfactory hallucinations described as a strong smell of burnt rubber followed by an epigastric rising sensation. These aura episodes typically last 20 to 40 seconds and resolve spontaneously without loss of awareness. She delivered her first child six weeks ago via uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been breastfeeding with partial formula supplementation. Her husband reports that today, approximately four hours prior to arrival, the patient was seated on the couch while holding the infant when she suddenly called out that she was smelling burnt rubber. He immediately took the infant from her arms. She then stared blankly ahead and began making repetitive lip-smacking and swallowing movements for approximately 15 seconds. Her right hand began rhythmically picking at her clothing. She then developed bilateral arm stiffening followed by generalized rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting approximately 70 seconds. She was incontinent of urine during the event. Post-ictally, she was confused and drowsy for approximately 25 minutes before gradually becoming oriented again. The patient reports that her seizure frequency had been slowly increasing over the past several months, particularly since the third trimester of pregnancy, and she has had approximately five aura episodes in the past month alone compared to her baseline of two to three per year. She attributes this increase to sleep deprivation associated with caring for a newborn, though she continued her topiramate unchanged throughout pregnancy and postpartum. She denies any recent medication changes, missed doses, illness, fever, or head trauma. No other family members have been ill. She reports persistent fatigue and occasional headaches attributed to sleep deprivation but denies any new neurological symptoms.
